subtitle: Lesson 2 · AI and LLM Security Fundamentals

steps.label: Prompt Injection
steps.sub: Attacker input makes the model ignore instructions — direct or indirect

steps.label: Insecure Output Handling
steps.sub: Trusting LLM output as safe without validating it downstream

steps.label: Training Data Poisoning
steps.sub: Corrupted training/fine-tuning data teaches attacker-chosen behavior

steps.label: Model Denial of Service
steps.sub: Inputs crafted to exhaust compute or context-window resources

steps.label: Supply Chain Vulnerabilities
steps.sub: Risk inherited from third-party models, datasets, or plugins

steps.label: Sensitive Information Disclosure
steps.sub: Memorized or connected data leaking out in model output

steps.label: Insecure Plugin Design
steps.sub: Tools an LLM calls with no validation or access control of their own

steps.label: Excessive Agency
steps.sub: An agent with more permissions than its task needs

steps.label: Overreliance
steps.sub: Trusting LLM output as authoritative without verification

steps.label: Model Theft
steps.sub: Unauthorized copying or exfiltration of proprietary model weights

code:
# Most of these trace to ONE root cause:
#
# No reliable boundary between:
#   trusted instructions <-> untrusted content   (input side)
#   probabilistic output  <-> something to trust  (output side)
#
# Prompt Injection + Insecure Output Handling
#   = that same gap, seen from input and output
# Excessive Agency + Insecure Plugin Design
#   = that gap wired directly into real actions
caption: Learn the root cause once, and the list stops feeling like ten unrelated items.
